# What's the Key?

## Reports or Events?

```{python}
#| echo: true
stories = [('BBC','Chibok'), ('CNN','Chibok'),
           ('Japan Times','Chibok'), ('SaharaReporters','Chibok')]

counts = {}
for outlet, event in stories:
  counts[event] = counts.get(event, 0) + 1

print(len(stories))
print(counts)
```

Four kidnappings, or one kidnapping reported four times?

::: {.notes}

Illustrative data, not GDELT's: the outlets are the ones that D'Ignazio and Klein name on p.2.

Same data, two keys. Count by *story* and you get 4; count by *event* and you get 1. Remember from Dictionaries: "the key is unique. Always." The choice of key *is* the choice of what you're counting.

Then the next slide.

:::

```python
my_cities = [

  ['New York', 40.7127, 74.0059, -5],
  ['Tokyo', 35.6833, 139.6833, +8]

```

What's wrong with this data?

:::

## The Numbers Don't Speak for Themselves

| | On my slide | Actually |
| :-- | --: | --: |
| London longitude | `0.1275` | `-0.1275` |
| New York longitude | `74.0059` | `-74.0059` |
| Tokyo time zone | `+8` | `+9` |
| New York time zone | `-5` | `-5` (winter), `-4` (summer) |

. . .

> "'Raw data' is an oxymoron" ~ Gitelman and Jackson, quoted in @dignazio:2020ch6 [p.13]

::: {.notes}

These numbers have been in my videos for years. Nobody spotted them, because numbers on a slide look authoritative. Those who did spot them had *context*: they know where New York is.

The New York time zone isn't even wrong: it's *incomplete*. The structure has nowhere to say "when".

If time: in `ds2` the keys are the *only* metadata, so a Python dictionary's keys are a (very thin) data dictionary. Is `tz` in hours? Is it summer time? D'Ignazio and Klein (p.6): "If you are lucky you might get [...] a data dictionary that describes what each column [...] means." My margin note on p.6 ("Most data arrive on our computational doorstep context-free"): the problems I've had with EPC data (≤ 60 seconds).

:::

# Break It, Then Fix It

## Why the Command Line?

The last 100,000 crimes reported to Chicago police in 2025 (28MB)^[Downloaded via `curl -L -o crimes2025.csv 'https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/t7ek-mgzi.csv?$limit=100000&$order=date%20DESC'`]:

```bash
wc -l crimes2025.csv                 # how many rows?
head -2 crimes2025.csv               # what are the columns?
cut -d, -f6 crimes2025.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
```

. . .

About two seconds for 100,000 rows, and no Python.

::: {.notes}

**Download it beforehand.** It took about 40 seconds on home broadband (16 Oct). Show the command, but don't run it on the room's wifi. The server sometimes returns an empty file with no error (it happened once on 16 Oct): check with `wc -l` and run it again if you get 0.

`curl -L -o crimes2025.csv 'https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/t7ek-mgzi.csv?$limit=100000&$order=date%20DESC'`

This is the city's API, as in the Python slide, with a limit and a fixed order (latest first: 30 July to 31 December 2025). Without `$limit` the API stops at 1,000 rows; with it set to 300,000 you get the whole year (238,150 rows, 69MB, about a minute). Don't use the portal's "Export" link (`/api/views/.../rows.csv`): it's deprecated and the server says it stops on 22 December 2026.

This is the "Crimes - 2025" extract (`t7ek-mgzi`). The 2022 one the course used before is `9hwr-2zxp`. The full "Crimes - 2001 to Present" (`ijzp-q8t2`) is too big to demo.

As of 16 Oct: top types THEFT 22,988, BATTERY 18,038, CRIMINAL DAMAGE 11,395. The API puts every field in quotes, so the output reads `"THEFT"`. Records are revised daily, so re-run before class.

**Why not Excel?** 100,000 rows will open (Excel's limit is 1,048,576; the 2001-to-present file is well over that). The real problem is what Excel does to the values: 66,222 of these rows have an IUCR crime code with a leading zero (`"0560"`), and Excel turns it into the number 560. `beat` (`"0931"`) and `district` (`"009"`) go the same way. Excel decides what the data mean as it opens the file, which is today's question.

This is the pay-off for week 2's CLI video: `|` chains small tools. The same pipe idea is behind `git log | grep`.

:::

## Is That Right?

```bash
grep -c '"HOMICIDE"' crimes2025.csv                    # 194
grep '"HOMICIDE"' crimes2025.csv | grep -c '"true"'    # arrests?
```

. . .

81 is wrong. The answer is 78.

. . .

```bash
awk -F, '{print NF}' crimes2025.csv | sort | uniq -c   # 22 columns?
```

::: {.notes}

Ask the room (pairs, 1 minute) before revealing: "Is 81 the number of homicides with an arrest?"

Why it's wrong: `arrest` and `domestic` are both `"true"`/`"false"` columns next to each other. `grep '"true"'` also matches the 3 homicides with no arrest that were domestic. (Checked with Python's `csv` module: 78 arrested, 116 not.)

The `awk` line: most rows have 22 fields, but about 1,800 have 23–25, because descriptions like "AGG. DOMESTIC BATTERY - HANDS, FISTS, FEET, SERIOUS INJURY" contain commas inside quotes. `cut -d,` doesn't know about quotes. Column 6 happens to come before the problem, so the first count was right, but only by luck.

Back to the week's question: the storage format (CSV, and someone's choice of description text) decides what a quick tool can see. The CLI is fast; it isn't clever.

Two more data biography points if time:

- `updated_on`: about 193,000 of the 238,150 rows for 2025 were revised in 2026. A 'record' is not fixed when it's written.
- The city says the data shouldn't be used to compare over time, because classifications change after preliminary reporting. These are *reports*, as with GDELT.

:::

## From CSV to a Dict of Lists

```python
import csv
import urllib.request

url = 'https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/t7ek-mgzi.csv?$limit=20'

with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as f:
    rows = list(csv.reader(f.read().decode('utf-8').splitlines()))

header = rows[0]   # the column names
data   = rows[1:]  # a list of lists: one list per crime

crimes = {}        # a dict of lists: one list per column
for col in ['date', 'primary_type', 'block', 'arrest', 'latitude']:
    i = header.index(col)
    crimes[col] = []
    for row in data:
        crimes[col].append(row[i])
```

::: {.notes}

Copy and modify: this runs as-is in the SDS container, with no download. The `?$limit=20` asks the city's API for just 20 rows. (The API's column names are lower case with underscores, unlike the CSV export: `primary_type`, not `Primary Type`.)

Don't explain the first block (`with`, `urlopen`, `decode`): "this gets the file; we'll see how in a later week". The part to walk through is the bottom half: the 3.2 list of lists becomes the 3.3 dict of lists. `header.index(col)` is the same trick as `ds2['name'].index('Tokyo')`.

Invite them to change the column list, or `$limit=20` to `$limit=100`.

:::

## Ask the Data

In pairs, write down the code *before* I run it:

1. How many of the 20 led to an arrest?
2. What is the average `latitude`?
3. Look at rows 2 and 4. One crime or two?

::: {.notes}

Switch to JupyterLab in the container. Ask a pair for the code for each one, type what they say, and run it (wrong code is fine: the error is the lesson).

Answers as of 16 Oct (the API returns the latest rows first; re-run before class):

1. `crimes['arrest'].count('true')` → 4. **Trap:** the values are the *strings* `'true'` and `'false'`, not `True`/`False`, so `crimes['arrest'].count(True)` gives 0.
2. `sum(crimes['latitude'])` → `TypeError`: everything is a string. Someone has to *decide* it's a number: `float(...)` in a loop. Back to the week's question: the CSV doesn't store meaning, so you have to supply it.
3. Both are PUBLIC PEACE VIOLATION, "OTHER VIOLATION", on an AIRCRAFT at 100XX W OHARE ST, at 23:54 on New Year's Eve, with different case numbers (JK100014, JK100011). Two reports of one incident, or two incidents? You can't tell from the data. That's GDELT again. (Rows 9 and 10 are similar: a theft and a credit card fraud at the same place and time.)

Cut for time, but use if you're ahead: "What was the first crime, and where?" (`crimes['primary_type'][0]`, `crimes['block'][0]` → ASSAULT, 050XX S PAULINA ST) and "Where was the first `THEFT`?" (`crimes['block'][crimes['primary_type'].index('THEFT')]` → 006XX E GRAND AVE, row 9: the "time zone of Tokyo" pattern from the DOLs video).

:::

# Gitting More<br />Out of Life

## Break It

```bash
git rm fileA.md
git commit -m "Removed file."
ls                       # fileA.md has gone
git log --oneline        # find the hash before the removal
git checkout <hash>
ls                       # fileA.md is back
```

::: {.notes}

Live, in the SDS container: the Recovery slide from the Git video, done for real. Set up the repo beforehand (README → fileA.md → commit, as in the video).

Ask before running `git checkout`: "What will `git status` say now?"

:::

## Detached HEAD

```bash
git status               # HEAD detached at <hash>
git switch -             # back to the branch you were on
```

To bring *one* file back into the present:

```bash
git restore --source=<hash> fileA.md
git commit -m "Restored fileA.md"
```

::: {.notes}

This is the "getting back to HEAD" discussion that the Git video promises but never delivers.

`git switch -` works whether your branch is `main` or `master`. GitHub now defaults to `main`, but the video slides say `master`.

:::

## Commits on a Plane

| | CVS (1990), Subversion (2000) | Git (2005) |
|---|---|---|
| Where is the history? | On one central server | In every copy |
| Commit offline? | No | Yes |
| GitHub is… | (n/a) | just another copy |

. . .

So `commit` and `push` are *different* things.

::: {.notes}

The point the video doesn't make: Git is peer-to-peer. Every clone is a complete repository, with the full history. GitHub is a copy that everyone has agreed to treat as the main one; Git itself doesn't know that.

Keep this to a 1-minute aside; the history is optional. The history: CVS and then Subversion ("CVS done right") were centralised: you needed the server to commit. The Linux kernel moved to BitKeeper, a proprietary distributed system, in 2002. In April 2005 the free licence was withdrawn after a dispute over reverse-engineering its protocol, and Linus Torvalds wrote Git in a matter of days to replace it. (Mercurial started that same month for the same reason.)

Why it's weird: there's no single 'true' copy, so `pull` and `push` are needed to make copies agree. Why it's useful: you can commit on a plane, and the history survives if GitHub disappears.

This sets up the next slide: a commit on your laptop is not a backup until you push.

:::

## Pull, Then Push

```bash
git pull                 # get any changes from GitHub first
git add <notebook.ipynb>
git commit -m "What I did, and why"
git push                 # only now are you backed up
```

When asked for a password, GitHub wants a **personal access token** (or an SSH key), not your account password.

::: {.notes}

The video's workflow slide leaves out `pull`, but the learning outcome includes it.

Why the command line rather than a GUI: it shows what's happening behind the scenes. `add` and `commit` are *separate* steps, and a GUI usually hides that. The separation is the point: you choose what goes into the record.

Everyone should have a GitHub account by now. The first `push` from the command line is where the password prompt catches people out.

Link back to 3.6: in the group project you'll be pulling and pushing to *one* repository with up to four other people, and the commit history is how we see who did what if a group falls out.

Spare question if time: "You commit, and then your laptop is stolen. Is your work on GitHub?" (No: all changes are local until pushed.) Story: the flatmate's laptop.

:::

## A Commit Message Is Context

> The way through this predicament is by considering context, a process that includes understanding the provenance and environment from which the data was collected [...] ~ @dignazio:2020ch6 [p.27]

. . .

`git log` is the provenance of *your* work. Write the message for the person who will read it in six months.

::: {.notes}

D'Ignazio and Klein's "data biography" (p.24) asks five questions: Where did it come from? Who collected it? When? How was it collected? Why was it collected? A good commit history answers most of them for your own code. My margin note: "Something to think about for the assessment, perhaps?"


Bridge to the practical: the final commit of the notebook. Ask for a message that would make sense to a stranger.

:::

## Intro to the practical

Here's what we're covering:

- Bedding in your Git/GitHub workflow. We're trying to help you remember via repetition here and get good habits started early.
- Lists and dictionaries are the 'workhorse' data structures of Python: you'll use them all the time even once you know of other, more powerful ways to organise and manage data. You might, for instance, have a list of advanced data structures that you want to iterate over. Or a dictionary of parameters that you want to test in a model.
- We're also going to stretch your understanding of how these two data structures interrelate and, crucially, look at the DOL, which is analogous to how pandas — probably *the* single biggest reason Python dominates data science — manages and represents data to you.
